metadata.title: Interview With Dan Patrick of ESPN Radio

text: ENTITY, when I was walking over here, I mentioned to one member of your staff, Well, it must be a bittersweet time. And he bristled a little. He was gentlemanly about it, but he bristled a little. Do you see it as a bittersweet time? Well, only a little bit, actually. I am very happy and very much at peace and very grateful for the chance to serve and grateful especially that the country is in such good shape as I leave office. But I think, for all of us, it may be bittersweet in the sense that people- virtually everybody that works here likes the work, and we tried never to forget that it was a job and that we were privileged to do it. But everything comes to an end; you have to do something else. And I think we have had our time here. I am just focused on doing everything I can in the days that remain, helping President-elect Bush have a successful transition and kind of savoring and being grateful for the good things that have happened. The country is still in the midst of an almost 8-year boom. The country is at peace. You have had, by many measurements, if not most-perhaps even all measurements-at least a reasonably successful Presidency. Why are we having a Republican President come in behind you? Well, I think partly because of the prosperity. I think they both debated how to use the prosperity, and the country was evenly divided. One candidate won the popular vote, and the Supreme Court decided the electoral vote. People will be analyzing that for years to come. Maybe I will have a chance to analyze it, too, after some time. But I do not know that I have anything to add to what is been said by others. Maybe we ought to come back to that later. Through most of the 8 years of your Presidency, you and your Vice President seemed to all the world to be joined at the hip. There were historians who were writing that Vice President Gore had been given as much or more responsibility than any Vice President in the history of the country. Oh, more. There is no question about that. And that he did a very good job as Vice President. And he did. I think that when the period of this history is written and people who care about American Government look at how we organized and ran the administration, they will say a number of things, including the fact that we came here with a well-thoughtout set of ideas and policies, and we basically did what we said we'd do in '92 and then again in '96, and that we had a real team operation in the White House, and that the Vice President had more responsibility in more areas than any Vice President in history and carried them out very well. I do not think there is any question that in the job of Vice President, he is the most effective person that has held that job and had more responsibility than anyone who ever had it. That being the case, ENTITY, when he, in effect, ran away from you during the campaign, you had to be disappointed at that. Well, I think, first of all, everybody has got to run their own race. And it is a difficult thing running as Vice President. There is no accident that only two Vice Presidents in the history of the country have ever been directly elected President. If you get to be Vice President, you have got an excellent chance of getting to be President, because something could happen to the President, and you have got a terrific chance of being the nominee for President of your party. But to be directly elected, it is only happened twice. And once, when Martin Van Buren succeeded Andrew Jackson, we were still virtually a oneparty country. And the only other time it happened was in 1988, when basically there was an enormously contentious and negative campaign which succeeded in painting the Democratic nominee, Governor Dukakis, as virtually un-American. This was basically a pretty positive campaign. They had a debate about what to do. They talked about the various issues, and the people split. But back to the question-had to feel disappointed? I really believe every person has to decide what is best for them. And I thought that it was-let me just say, I thought that it was the right thing for me not to be out there very much until the end, the last week or 10 days. I did most of what I could do early by going to scores of events for our House and Senate candidates and for the Democratic Party, which helped the Vice President, of course, directly, the Democratic Party work did. And when a Vice President becomes a President, he tries to figure out some way to establish his own identity and to get the benefit of the good things that have happened, but still to be an independent person. And I do not think that anybody else should second-guess that. Once your party has a nominee, then the rest of us should be on the team. I think politics is a team sport. It is about addition, not subtraction. And I do not believe the rest of us should secondguess the leader of the team, including me. Do you agree or disagree that some of your failures, policy as well as personal failures in the White House, had an impact on Al Gore's losing? Yes, to the first; no, to the second. To say that people would hold him responsible for any personal mistake I made is an insult to the American people. I mean, people just are not that unfair. The people of this country are basically good people. And moreover, there were a lot of surveys along toward the end of the campaign that showed that if I could have run again, I would have done fine. So I just do not think there is any evidence of that. On the policies, however, there were-you know, I do not know if the fact that we drew the short straw and had that terrible mess with the Elian Gonzalez case cost him a lot of votes in Florida, but it could have. And if it did, I feel very badly about it, because this was not anything anybody dreamed up. I do not think there is any question that a number of-in West Virginia, some people voted against him in the northern part of the State because they blamed us-I do not think they are right about it, but they did blame us for the closing of a steel mill there that occurred more or less at the same time of the Asian financial crisis. They thought we should have moved more quickly than we did to stop the inflow of cheap steel. I do not think there is-I do not know if you'd call this a policy failure, but I do not think there is any doubt that in at least five States I can think of, the NRA had a decisive influence because they disagreed with our attempts to close the gun show loophole and have child trigger locks, safety locks, and ban large-scale ammunition clips. You know, presumably, some people voted for him because we were for those things. But one of the sad things about all gun safety legislation is that people tend to vote for the issues, but when they are voting for candidates, the antis tend to be more intense than the pros. I mean, if you look at Colorado, which is basically a Republican State now, the Vice President lost there, but closing the gun show loophole passed 70-30. In Oregon, because of the Nader candidacy, he only won a narrow victory, but the gun show loophole closing carried 2-1. So I think you have to give the-so the policy issues that we fought out, I do not think there is any question they cost him some votes. I think that, on balance, I believe he gained more because of the economic success of the administration, because we have 8 years in a row of declining crime, because the welfare rolls were cut in half, because of the millions of people that were benefited by family leave, because of the things we did. So I think, on balance, it was more of a plus than a minus by a good long way; two-thirds of the people thought the country was going in the right direction. But in a race like this that is so close, you think about some of the issues we had in West Virginia on that steel mill or the Gonzalez case, and you wonder-I mean, President Kennedy once said that victory has a thousand fathers, and defeat is an orphan. In this case, where the Vice President won the popular vote and, by decision of the Supreme Court, lost the electoral college, defeat may have a thousand fathers, too. We will all be chewing over this for- heck, people will be writing about this 100 years from now. I have so much ground I want to cover with you, about your legacy, about the future, and I do not intend to spend the rest of our time talking about the election just finished. But anyone who is ever been around a courthouse knows that judges, high and low, frequently engage in raw politics-all hope they will deal with the law. You mentioned earlier the Supreme Court. To those who are absolutely convinced that the Supreme Court, they just had a Republican majority, wanted a Republican as President, and voted politics, not the law-as an attorney and as our President, you say what? I say, when I get out and start teaching constitutional law again, I will tell you exactly what I think about it. The important vote there, the 5-4 vote-there were actually three separate opinions, but the 5-4 vote was a vote to stop the vote count-- That was the clincher. --6 days in advance of the electoral college meeting. And the American people will just have to make their own decisions about it. But I think that it will be viewed in history as a momentous decision, and I think that it will be debated a long time. But it is very interesting. You know, there is a lot of stuff already been written about it. I noticed there were three articles in this week's Economist about it, basically critical, even though the Economist endorsed President-elect Bush. There is going to be a lot of stuff written about it. But I think that from my point of view, as long as I am President, what I should be focused on doing is telling the country that we should accept it, because the principle of judicial review has served us well. And all of us believe, looking back in history, that there were periods when the Supreme Court made serious mistakes, but when they did, they normally were corrected over time. So I think the Vice President spoke for all of us when he said he strongly disagreed with the decision, but he accepted it. And right now we need to focus on pulling the country together, giving President-elect Bush a chance to get off to a good start, to hit the ground running, dealing with all these issues that are out there. And there will be lots of time for me and others to say exactly what the elements of the Supreme Court decision were. But I just do not think I should say more than that now. We are going to move on and talk about the economy. Before doing so, as one who taught law, as an attorney, were you surprised that this Supreme Court ever took the case? I ask this, again, for backdrop. Many attorneys I have talked to, of all persuasion and all parties, said they were surprised-some say stunned-that this Court would have even taken the case. Well, let me say, I think most lawyers-or a lot of them-are surprised they took the case. Even those that were surprised they took the case were shocked when the vote count was stopped on the Friday. Were you? No. No, not after 8 years in Washington, I was not . But I had not found a single lawyer who believes that there is precedent any time in American history for it. I have asked probably 50, 60. But I was not surprised, no. They had the power to do it, and they did it. And it is done, and we should accept it, because the country has to go on. We cannot reverse the principle of judicial review, and we should not . And we should try to help the President-elect get off to a good start, give him a chance to govern the country. I hope he will be given a decent honeymoon. I know what it is like not to have one, and I hope he will get one. And I think we should-we ought to just- right now, everybody can think what they think about it, but for me, I believe I owe my country. The people of this country have been good to me, and I have had a chance to serve in this job. It is hard enough under the best circumstances. The President-elect won the electoral college, and he deserves a chance to have a good start. And that is what I am going to focus on, and I am going to try to give it to him. Let us talk about the economy. I think, by any reasonable analysis, that the incoming Bush administration is trying to position the economic picture in the following way: The economy is starting downward, maybe headed toward a recession, and therefore they are positioning themselves to be able to say, whatever happens on the downside, particularly if we have a recession, Do not forget, it is the Clinton/Gore administration, not this new incoming administration. Well, they do that. You know, you cannot blame them for trying to buy low and sell high if they want to try to do that. But I personally believe that no one knows how long we can keep this recovery going. But the overwhelming majority of the experts believe that we are going to have a pretty good year next year. Now, it is already the longest economic expansion in history. We had over 22 million new jobs. I do not think you can totally repeal the business cycle, but it is certain that it is changed. And what has changed it? First of all, you have to give the American people a lot of credit here. You have this explosion of entrepreneurial energy, not only among small businesses and dot-com companies but people integrating technology and productivity into big old traditional firms. There is no question that technology has enabled productivity to grow much more rapidly than in the past, and that keeps these recoveries going. And we have kept interest rates down, and we continue to invest in the education and training of the American people. And we continue to open new markets around the world and at home. Those are the things that I think are important for the Government to do. Now, for the last couple of years, we were growing at a blistering pace. In other words, we have been growing ever since I got here, but we have been growing at a blistering pace. No one believed we could continue to grow at 5 percent a year. Most people believe next year growth will be around 3 percent. And I believe that the important thing is to just keep following a solid economic policy. I think we can have a tax cut; I have always said that. But I think it needs to be modest enough so that there is no question that we are going to continue to pay down the debt and pay it off within a decade or so, at least 12 years. I think that will keep interest rates down. That is a big tax cut to ordinary people and to business people and to investors, because it keeps the market up and it keeps inflation down. Then I think it is important to save back enough money to invest what we have to invest in education and our other responsibilities, including national security. I think it is important to save back enough money to deal with the long-term challenges to Medicare and Social Security. You have got the baby boom generation about to retire. And depending on what you decide to do with it, it costs more or less money to do it. But I think that-there is no question that we can. I believe we should have a tax cut. The question is, how big should it be, and whether you can meet your other obligations? But the most important thing people want is to keep this economy going. And I think, you know, it is got quite a little life left in it, I think. Quite a bit of life left in it, you say. ENTITY, with respect, you know as I know that in politics, a lot of it is trying to pin a tail on somebody else. This economy goes down even a little, it is fairly clear that the tail is going to be-at least they will try to pin the tail on you. Well, they will have the microphone, of course. But I think that what-the American people hire us not so much to place blame as to produce. And over the long run, that is how we are all judged, I think. And I do not think any-at least no economist thought we could continue to grow at 5 percent a year indefinitely. Are you in favor of interest rates staying low, or do you think they need to be raised some or lowered some? Oh no, I think-well, no, no, no. I think-I like low interest rates, which is why we have been paying the debt down. Now, if the Federal Reserve believes that the economy is slowing too much, they might want to cut short-term rates again and try to get a little more investment going. And I think that that is something that they have under consideration. I have found that, basically, Chairman Greenspan has had a pro-growth policy. He is tried to see this economy grow as much as it could without inflation. On a couple of occasions over the last 8 years, he may have made a call different than I would have made it, but on the whole, I think he is managed this thing in a responsible way, and I have tried to manage my part of it in a responsible way. And that is enabled us to have the longest expansion in history with low inflation. You know, I'd just like to-when I took office, the deficit of this country-the debt had quadrupled, and the deficit was $295 billion. This year we are going to pay off-we will have paid off, in the last 3 years, $360 billion on the national debt. And I just learned, about 30 minutes before we started this interview, that with the budget we finished last weekend, we are going to pay off another $200 billion on the national debt. So we will have paid down $560 billion on the national debt over 4 years. Now, that is a huge impact to keep interest rates low and growth high. So I still think they can-if this thing is managed properly, I think they will have some more growth here. Now, like I said, I do not know- no one knows how much you can combine the entrepreneurial spirit of the American people, the explosion of technology and productivity growth, and proper Government policies, and how long you can keep this going. No one knows the answer to that, but I think they can- I think we can keep it going quite a while longer. So to move on, are you in favor or not in favor of cutting interest rates now? For 8 years, I have refused to second-guess the Fed publicly, and I do not think I should change as I am going out the door. The press indicates that they have that under advisement, that they are thinking about it. And it is something I think they ought to think about. It depends upon what the data shows about how much they think the economy is slowing. Everyone-they wanted-the Fed's raised interest rates, you remember. They knew it had to slow some. If we kept growing at 5 percent a year, there was too big a risk we'd have an explosion in inflation or an explosion of interest rates or both. But then we had the increased fuel prices, which slowed things down some, and a few other developments and some corrections in some of the high-tech stocks. So I think they have got it under consideration. I think that if they do it, I think it will certainly be an understandable decision. But my point is, the thing that keeps interest rates really low is the fact that we are paying the debt off. That will keep interest rates low, inflation low, and if we keep investing in education, investing in technology, investing in scientific research, staying on the cutting edge of change, and opening new markets around the world-something I think that this incoming administration and I agree on-I think that we have got quite a bit of life left in the economy. The American people are still working hard, and they are very innovative. So I expect them to have a good year next year. Let us have some fun. If you could recommend one book that the incoming President, George Bush, should read, what would it be? That is hard. But if it were only one book, I'd probably tell him to read David Herbert Donald's biography of Abraham Lincoln. If you could recommend he see one movie that you think might help him in his years here, however long they would be, what would that be? High Noon, because Gary Cooper does the right thing, even when people leave him, and even though he is scared, he does not pretend to be macho. He is scared to death, and he does the right thing anyway. You are not going to believe this, but when I went over with my staff what your answer would be, I told them, High Noon. I want you to check it later. Let us move along. When you look back over your 8 years, what is the one thing now that you wish you had known 8 years ago? Oh, boy, that is hard to answer. There are so many things I wish I had known 8 years ago. But I wish I had understood better, 8 years ago, exactly how what I do here both is seen by and reacted to by Congress and by the American people, better than I did then. I could give you lots of examples, but I think if I had done that, I think a lot of the-some of the early conflicts that I had would have been different. I also wish I had understood better than I did when I came here the different views generally held by the two parties on the nature of political power and its uses in Washington- ways that I just did not understand then. Your finest hour as President? That is very, very hard to say. I had a lot of great times, for which I am very grateful. But I think when we prevailed in both Houses by one vote on the economic plan in '93, that is what really turned the economy around and made possible so much else that happened. If we had not had a functioning economy, I do not believe the welfare reform efforts would have worked as well as they have; I do not think the family leave law would have benefited 25 million people; I doubt if the crime rate would have gone down for 8 years in a row, even though we had a good crime policy; and I am not sure I would have had the support from the American people to end the ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Kosovo, or be involved as I was in Northern Ireland, the Middle East, a lot of other places. We might have had too much trouble here at home for me to do that. It probably-the fact that we had that lonely battle that only succeeded by one vote probably made so much else possible. Your darkest hour? I have had more than one of them, too. But certainly one of them was when those 18 American soldiers were killed in Somalia. It was awful, because of the circumstances, which I hope to be able to talk about in some detail someday. But to lose them all in what was a humanitarian mission, because they were asked to try to arrest a person who had been responsible for killing our Pakistani comrades who were there also on a humanitarian mission, and then to wind up with all those Somalis dead and losing 18 of our people, it was a dark day. Impeachment had to be a dark day. Well, by the time they got around to voting, I knew what was going to happen. And I did not -no, my darkest day came long before that when I had to come to terms with the fact that I made a terrible personal mistake, which I tried to correct in private and which then got dragged into public. That was dark for me. By the time they got around to voting on impeachment, I knew what it was, and it did not have any-I felt that to me, if we could defeat impeachment, it was like the second big battle of the Gingrich revolution. The first was when they shut the Government down, and that was the second one. That does not mean that I did not make a terrible mistake, but there were 800 people, including a lot of Republicans, who were legal and constitutional scholars, who wrote a letter saying this was not an impeachable offense and should not even be considered. And they all knew that, too. That was a political battle we were involved in. I did not seek it. I did not want to fight it, but I was only too happy to take it up, because I believe the real purpose of it was to try to weaken me and our side and what we believed in, and to strengthen their side and what they believed in. In that, they succeeded. Well, I am not sure they did. In 1998 we won seats in the House of Representatives for the first time since 1822 in the sixth year of a President's term. So I am not sure they did. It may be that, after the fact, that what they did will acquire some historical legitimacy. But what I regret about that was what I did wrong, not the fact that they impeached me, because that was wrong, too. I agreed with Joe Lieberman, as I said at the time. I agreed with what he said, that what I did was wrong and what they did was wrong. And I think that is the way history will record it. ENTITY, the clock rolls. Allow me to pick up the pace a little. I want to read you off a list and ask you to tell me the first thing that comes into your mind. President-elect. Like him? I do not know him very well. I like his father very much, and I have actually had more contact with his brother, who is the Governor of Florida, than I have with him. But I have a lot of friends in Texas who like him, who say he is a good man, like his wife very much, like his daughters. And I hope he will succeed. We will go down the list, and we will stop on each one. Best Vice President this country ever had, a partner who without I could not have been successful as President. Newt Gingrich. A brilliant adversary and a complicated man. A bit of an adversary? Brilliant. A brilliant adversary. Brilliant adversary. And a complicated man. He is a complicated man, interesting man. The National Rifle Association. An effective adversary, but I think, on balance, a negative force, because they are trying to convince their people that we are trying to do something we are not trying to do. Which is? Take everybody's guns away. That is why I like giving speeches in debate with them, because I always tell everybody I talk to, if you missed a day in the deer woods or a single sport shooting contest, you ought to vote against me and our whole crowd. But if you did not , they must be telling you something that is not true here. Let us look at what we are really for. So I think the NRA did a lot of good things in Arkansas when I was there-hunter education programs; they helped me resolve some property disputes. They really did some good things, but now they are just into terrifying people and building their membership and raising money. And it is just not true we are trying to take their guns away. It is just not true that we have interfered with legitimate hunters and sports people. And it is just not true that we have done enough in America to protect people from the dangers of criminals and kids having guns. But you have got to give it to them; they have done a good job. They have probably had more to do than anyone else in the fact we did not win the House this time, and they hurt Al Gore. Going on down the list, Janet Reno. Good woman, tried really hard to do a good job. She is a good person. Your mother. First thing that comes to my mind? I still miss her every day. Hillary Rodham Clinton. I love her, and I am really proud of her. Chelsea. I love her, and I am really proud of her. Do you expect her to run for something some day? Oh, Lord, I kind of doubt it. Although, I am proud of her; she got into this deal helping her mom, and she traveled with me some when Hillary could not go the last year and 3 or 4 months. She cares about public issues and public life, and she is got a big heart. And she is really interested in all of it, but I do not know that she would ever run for office. But if she did, if she wanted to do it, I'd sure support her and do whatever I could to help her. But it is totally up to her. The Lincoln Bedroom. It is the place where Lincoln freed the slaves. Whitewater. Biggest bogus issue in modern American politics-classic. It was a fraud from the get-go, and a lot of the people that were propagating it knew it was a fraud. And in that sense, people will look at this years from now and be amazed that anybody rode it as hard as they did for as long as they did. Special Prosecutor Kenneth Starr. Independent Counsel. First title is better than the second. But I do not have any-he just did what he was supposed to do. I do not have any particular bad feelings about him. He did what he was supposed to do? Yes. What was he supposed to do? They put him in there because Fiske was a fair, balanced man, and the whole thing was going to be over before the '96 election, and they did not want that. And so they put him in there, said, Drag it out and get a bigger body count. And that is -he just did what he was supposed to do. But I do not really have any-that group, that faction of the Republican Party controlled those independent counsels, and that is what they did. But I do not have any personal animosity toward him like that. I mean, he really-he is part of that crowd, and they really believe it. They think that whatever they do to our side is okay, and that is what they really believe. I did not -I underestimated that when I got here. I just did not really believe it. I always had good relationships with Republicans at home, even very conservative ones, members of the so-called Christian right. We always dealt with issues head up. And I just did not understand that before I got here, but once I figured out what the deal was, I could sort of let it go. I realized they just had a different world view than I did. At the end of my list-well, first, the Republican leadership on Capitol Hill. We got a lot done together and could have gotten more done if they had not given their rightwingers veto power from time to time. For example, we had-look what we got done this year. We just passed the best education budget of my entire 8 years as President, huge increases for after-school programs, school modernization and repair, nearly doubled the number of kids in the after-school programs, big increase in Head Start. We have now done more to expand college access than anything since the GI bill. We passed the China trade bill, the Africa-Caribbean Basin trade bill. And we took the earnings limit off of Social Security. We did a bunch of stuff this year, and we did for the last 6 years. But we have a majority in the Congress- in this Congress, not the new one coming in, in the one that went out-we had a majority for campaign finance reform. We had a majority for a Patients' Bill of Rights. We had a majority for an increase in the minimum wage. I believe we had a majority for closing the gun show loophole. But you could not get that through. No, because the rightwing blocked the leadership from letting us have a full and fair vote on that. So that I regret. But I worked with them, and I have very-personally, I like Senator Lott; I like Speaker Hastert. I have even acquired-- Do you like Tom DeLay? I have even acquired a rather jovial relationship with Dick Armey. We have gotten to where we joke around with each other. I think-Tom DeLay I do not know as well. I told him, I said, the only thing he ever said about me that really hurt my feelings was when he said he did not believe my golf handicap was as low as it was. And I sent him-I think I sent him a score that was in the Syracuse newspaper. But Tom DeLay worked with Hillary. They both got an award-Tom DeLay and Hillary both got an award from an adoption group because they'd done so much to try to facilitate adoptions. And that is the one area that I found real common ground with him on, that I think he is really genuine on. My problem with him is, his whole view about how you should treat your opponents is very different from mine. I just think he is got a total scorch-and-burn policy: take them out, whatever the cost, whatever you have to do. And he is real nice about it. If you smile, you'd have a very cordial conversation with him. I think he really believes that. I think he thinks that is the way you are supposed to treat your political opponents. And I just do not agree with that. For example, I never would have sent-I would not let someone from the White House go to a contested State and try to intimidate vote counters. I would not do that. I just do not believe that. That is not who I am. I do not think-I think that a great country has to have some voluntary restraint on the exercise of authority. But he is a very able guy, and if you do not stand up to him, he will run right over you. So he is a worthy adversary. At the end of my list-and you expect it-Monica Lewinsky. Sad chapter in my life that I wish were not public, but it is in the past. And for her, I wish her well. I hope she has a good life. Do you take the responsibility, the personal responsibility, full responsibility? Absolutely. I did, and I do. There was a report today you are thinking about hosting a television program. Anything to that? No. You guys make more money than I have, though. Maybe it is not a bad idea. I hear it costs a lot of money to support a Senator. Maybe I ought to look into it. Do not believe everything you read, ENTITY. I do not have an offer on the table. Is CBS getting into the bidding here? What about running for something? Are you going to run for mayor of New York? No. Governor of Arkansas? No. Governor of-- I loved it-no. Let me just say something about running. I think it is very important that-first of all, I need to take a couple of months and just go down. I need some rest. I have been working like crazy for 27 years. And I want to help Hillary, however I can, to succeed, because I think she-I am so proud of her, and I think she is immensely talented, and I think she will do very well. But I have got to support my family. I want to try- I have never had a chance to save any money. I want to try to save some, so they will be all right if anything happens to me. I have got to make sure we have paid all our bills. And I want to have some time to rest and just be a private citizen again. And then what I would like to do is to find a way to be a useful-to use all this incredible opportunity I have had as President to work on things that I care most about, here in the United States and around the world, but to do it in a way that does not in any inappropriate fashion get underfoot of the next President. I do not want to do that. I just want to try to be a good citizen. And I think there have been two truly great former Presidents in terms of their public service, John Quincy Adams and Jimmy Carter. John Quincy Adams because he went back and served in the House? He went back and served in the House, and he served 16 years-or served 8 terms, anyway-- Any chance you would do something like that? --and he is great. Well, let me finish. Then William Howard Taft went on the Supreme Court, served with some distinction. And for some years, Teddy Roosevelt kind of organized another political movement. Herbert Hoover did a lot of good. He went out and headed the commission for President Truman. So they also did well. Thomas Jefferson did some productive things after he left the White House. So there is evidence that if you do not just vegetate, you can do some good. And I am going to try to use my center and foundation to do some really good things. But I think that what I need to do is, I just need a little time to sort of decompress. And like I said, I want to try to take care of my family and just see what happens. But I care a lot-I just gave a speech in Coventry at the University of Warwick for Tony Blair, talking about, sort of, these big issues for the 21st century. Your globalization speech. Yes. How do you put a human face on a global economy? How do you empower poor people in America and around the world? What are we going to really do about AIDS and the breakdown of public health systems around the world? How are we going to figure out-how do you deal with global warming and still have economies growing? Unless we can break the link between putting more stuff into the air, greenhouse gases, and getting richer, we are going to have a disaster on our hands, because people are not going to agree not to become wealthier, and they should not . These big questions, these are things that I care about. I ran for the White House-sometimes I feel like a fish out of water, especially like this interview. We spent more than half our time on kind of like political questions. But the reason that I had some success as President, I am convinced more than anything else, is that I always thought Presidential elections and Presidential administrations were about ideas that resonated with the values of the American people but were appropriate to the present and the future. And I still believe that. If somebody asked me for advice, I'd say, Figure out what you believe, what is your vision of America; come up with a strategy to achieve it; then make your specific tactical move here. Decide what ideas you are going to push. I think that is very important. So when I am not President, that is what I think I ought to be doing, fighting for the things that I believe in, helping the people that I'd like to help, people that would be-people or problems that would be ignored by a lot of other people. So I hope I can do that. That is what I care about. And finally, of course, the great work of my life has been in racial and religious and ethnic reconciliation. And I have tried to carry it forward here as President. And I hope I will be able to make a contribution on that in the future. ENTITY, the clock is running quickly here. First of all, are you and the First Lady planning on selling the place in Chappaqua, New York? Gosh, I hope not. I have gone to a lot of trouble to fix that place up. Are you buying a place here in Washington, in Georgetown? I do not know. But you have got to have a place to live here. And I hope-we will either have to rent a place or buy a place, and we will figure out what to do about it. But-- Have not bought one yet? No, we have not bought one yet, and we are definitely not going to sell our place in Chappaqua if I have got anything to say about it. We have just got it all fixed up. We have done lots of work on that house. It is a delightful place. I am going to have an office, Presidential office, in New York City. I will have a-I will have my transition office here for 6 months, but I will have my permanent office up there. And I will have the home in Chappaqua, and I expect we will spend virtually all of our weekends there. But you have got to have a place to sleep down here. Now, the First Lady is going to be paid now-I will go to my notes here because this figure is a whopping figure-$8 million for her memoirs. What is she going to say about you in that book? I do not know. I do not know if there is $8 million worth to say. You all know it all already. But she is had two bestsellers, and she gave all the money away from the first one. The second is on the bestseller list, the book on the White House now. It is a really good book, I think. And she is given all the money away to that. So she just auctioned this one. I think she was probably as surprised as anybody that the auction brought that price. But the publisher that won it published her other bestsellers. I guess they think she is got a third one in her. I want to say this respectfully, ENTITY. Surely you do not want her writing about Paula Jones, Monica Lewinsky, and all those things again. Is she likely to do that? You ought to ask her. She can write about whatever she wants. I tell you, I bet it will be a good book. The First Lady's future. It is assumed among Democrats she is going to run for President. I guess the question is, does she do it in 2004 or 2008? Well, I will tell you what I believe. I believe that that is worse than idle speculation. I can tell you what I have urged her to do. What I have urged her to do is, number one, solidify her roots and her ties with the people of New York State; have an agenda for New York; have an agenda for America, because every Senator is a Senator on American issues, too; stay on the forefront of ideas, keep pushing and getting things done; and the future will take care of itself. But I think-she said she intends to serve her term in the Senate, and I believe that is what she intends to do. We already assume there are a lot of other people who will run for President again 4 years from now, including the Vice President. And of course, he would have a big leg up, because he won the popular vote this time. Do you consider him head of the Democratic Party now? I certainly think he is the leader of the party, and he won the election-the popular vote, I mean. He won the popular vote. And I think he will decide what he is going to do. Then other people will decide what they are going to do. But look, the world will look entirely different-could look different 6 months from now, a year from now. No one has any idea what it will be like 4 years from now. When I ran for President-this is why I said ideas are the most important-when I started running for President in late '91, my mother was about the only person who thought I could win. That is not quite true; Hillary did. But the incumbent President, President Bush, had an approval rating of over 70 percent. These things are not predictable. And I think people waste so much energy thinking about them and maneuvering. I want Hillary to enjoy being a Senator and to be the best Senator she can be. This seat was held by Senator Moynihan and Robert Kennedy, and they were great Senators. And that is what I want for her. You do, or do not, think it is a given that she will one day run for President? Oh, I do not think anything is a given like that. I do not think it is a given that any-if you could name me any person in this country, Democrat or Republican, and say, do you think it is a given that they will run for President, I would say no, because I do not . Abraham Lincoln once said about this-I think he'd always thought he'd run for President. He is the only person, apparently; we forgive his ambition. He once said, I will work and get ready, and perhaps my chance will come. That is about all anybody can do. But no, I do not know if any of them are going to run. ENTITY, I am so sorry to step on your line. I am so afraid time will run out on us. And you have been very generous with your time. Do you expect to be indicted after you leave the Presidency, by a current independent counsel, the successor to Kenneth Starr? Well, that is up to them. We had a bipartisan panel of prosecutors testified in the Congress that no ordinary prosecutor would do such a thing, would even think of it. There were five of them that testified to that. And the Republicans in the Congress argued that they did not have to have an indictable offense; you could impeach somebody for something that you would not indict them for. So I do not know. I may have more to say about that later. Look, I do not have any idea. I do not have any control over that, and I do not spend much time thinking about it. All I know is, Whitewater was a fraud; the civil lawsuit was a fraud. They knew that for a long, long time; everybody did. And a lot of innocent people have already been hurt for purely political reasons. And if I had to do it all over again, I still would, because the country is in better shape. So all I can tell you is, nothing can take away my feeling of gratitude for having had the chance to serve and my feeling of gratitude that it worked out so well for the American people. Do you think President Bush will pardon you to keep-possibly prevent an indictment, or in case of indictment? I have not given any thought to that. But I doubt it. I mean, no, I have not thought about that. There are those who say, Look, it would be a great unifying thing for the country, quote, unquote, for him to do that. Well, since I do not believe I should be charged, I do not want that. I will be happy to stand-I told you before, if that is what they want, I will be happy to stand and fight. Speaking of pardons, you still have your power to pardon people. True or untrue that you have considered pardons for the financier Milken, for Hubbell, for others involved in the Whitewater case, and for the killer of two FBI agents, Mr. Peltier? Any truth to that? I have been asked to consider pardons for hundreds and hundreds of people, and we are reviewing them all. And I will make decisions at an appropriate time. I do not want to discuss them until I make the decision about them. I will just mention one. On the Milken thing, the main thing I have heard from there is the people that are involved in prostate cancer, because he is been so active in that-I have heard a lot from people who say, He served his time. He paid a big price. You ought to do this because of the contribution he is made to the fight against prostate cancer. It sounds like you might-fair to say you might? No, it is not fair to say I will or I will not . I have not made a decision about that. Foreign policy, I wanted to talk to you about your legacy on foreign policy. This time it did not work out that way. Are you planning a trip to North Korea? I have not decided yet. We worked hard with North Korea. We made a big breakthrough there with the Secretary of State going. I'd like to do what I can to make sure that-we started this administration with the North Korea problem being the number one national security threat to the United States because of their nuclear program. We terminated that, and we are trying to figure out a way to terminate the missile program. If there was some way to do that, I might consider doing it. But I wanted to wait until we had a President-elect because they will have to have their own Korea policy. It may be something they prefer to do, maybe something they disagree with doing. So I just thought, while I do not think that the President-elect should have a veto- like I did not -President Bush went-did the Somalia thing after the election 8 years ago-I think it should be something that we discuss and we just try to work through what the best thing for America's interest is. Do you agree or disagree that U.S. policy in Cuba is out of step with your approach on other countries and has more to do with domestic policies and domestic politics than it does, actually, foreign policy? Well, I think it had a great deal to do with domestic policy and politics for a long time, in the sense that we have a lot of people in America who were personally hurt by the Castro regime and whose families were hurt and who lost their property, and they even lost their lives, lost their loved ones. So it is , in that sense, more personal. But I do not think there is any question that we would have made more progress with Cuba than we have if they had not shot those planes down and murdered those innocent people a few years ago. The Castro regime meaning Fidel, himself? Yes. They shot those Brothers to the Rescue planes down in blatant violation of international law. We do not believe they were in Cuban territorial waters. But even if they were in Cuban territorial waters, it was illegal. Cuba is a signatory to the Chicago convention, which specifically says how you have to handle planes like that. It governs what we do when we see planes take off from South America, small planes that we know are unarmed that may have drugs on them. A lot of times we have to follow them until they go down somewhere, or do that. What they did, it was a deliberate, illegal killing. That is a matter of foreign policy. Yes. And when they did that, the Congress reacted basically by passing the so-called Helms-Burton Act, which dramatically restricted the ability of any President to relax relations with Cuba. And it made me wonder if the person in the whole world that least wanted the embargo lifted was Fidel Castro. I mean, I have often wondered whether he and the people in America that do not want any change in relations are in some sort of unconscious dance with each other, because as long as that embargo is there, he is got an excuse for the failures of his regime. ENTITY, last question, China. There are reports out of China that they are razing church buildings, blowing them up, burning them down, on the eve of Christmas. And they have been doing this sort of thing for a year and a half. Are you now ready to recommend that the United States back this resolution at Geneva, before the United Nations Human Rights Commission, to condemn this kind of thing? Well, let me say, I have been- I have worked, I believe, as hard as any President for religious liberty at home and around the world, even for people who disagree with me on a lot of things. And I have had innumerable conversations with Jiang Zemin and with other Chinese officials about this. I think that their view that people who have strong religious convictions represent a political threat is just wrong. So I will do what I think is appropriate at the time on this. Does that include considering backing this resolution? I gave an answer. That is all the answer I want to give right now. ENTITY, you have been very generous with your time, and I appreciate it. Thank you, ENTITY. Thank you. Thank you.
